utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, have you now had the opportunity of going through the indictment, as amended, with your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is he ready to enter a plea?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll deal with that now. Mr. Kolundzija, would you stand, please. You have already entered pleas to this indictment, but because it's been amended, there are three counts, the first three counts which I must put to you again. You've discussed this with your counsel, and you're in a position to plead, are you? You understand the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED KOLUNDZIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Count 1, persecutions on political, racial or religious grounds, a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(h), 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal, how do you plead, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED KOLUNDZIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Count 2, inhumane acts, a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(1), 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute, how do you plead, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED KOLUNDZIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Count 3, outrages upon personal dignity, a violation of the laws or customs of war as recognised by Article 3(1)(c) of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, punishable under Articles 3, 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute, how do you plead, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED KOLUNDZIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The other matters having been sufficiently put, that concludes that. If you would like to sit down, Mr. Kolundzija. Mr. Vucicevic, I understand that there is no redacted copy of the indictment yet as confirmed, and if that be right -- have we got one?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's the issue of the confirmed - Yes, the actual confirmation, the document with the Judges' signature on it, that is what we don't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, and that's the whole -- because this was part and parcel of other matters at the time, there was an order for confidentiality of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see any difficulty about getting a redacted copy of it for our use.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours would appreciate having a copy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would do that within seven days, and serve it on the Defence too. Now, this matter will stand down. It will have to be adjourned. We have under consideration the matter of the joinder of this trial with another one. There will be a written judgement on that matter fairly shortly. Once that decision has been taken, no doubt other decisions can be taken about this particular trial. Mr. Niemann, is there anything you want to raise about this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, we will let you know when the decisions are out, you'll see them, and we'll let you know when the next appearance is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I may address the Court on two issues that are very critical to my representing my client before this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've got five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it too will be plenty. First, I have been thinking, you know, long and hard over the decision that the Court has taken yesterday, and it is -- I'm deeply concerned about the decision. If the decision says there was no written opinion of the Court, I'm not quite sure whether that decision is only based upon my administerial omissions and shortcomings, and in that case I do apologise and I would like to correct my behaviour from here on. However, if the decision is at all based on my integrity or character or fitness, perhaps that would deeply affect representation of my client, and if there is a scintilla of any doubt in Your Honours' minds about my willingness to faithfully serve this Court, then I would tender my resignation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The matter has been reported on the basis that you did not appear, as ordered in the scheduling order, at the hearing on Monday. Now, we can't go over that matter again. It's a matter which we shall refer to the Registrar, and you've got a transcript, of course, of what was said yesterday. Now, what was the next point?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: The next point is, you know, I haven't attended the hearing on the joinder of the indictments, and if I may present an oral argument on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we heard all the arguments. We've got your written submissions. You were absent on the occasion on which it should have been heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will allow you but only this: to allow anything which isn't in the written paper, isn't in the written paper. We don't want to hear a repetition of what is in the written paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my recent experience while investigating the matter in Prijedor, I have come into contact with many, many victims of the camps who clearly would like to come forward and testify. However -- this is amplifying it very great -- and adding a great weight to what I said in my written submission. However, they would not be willing to come and help the others whose behaviour and activities in the camps were not like Kolundzija's, number 1. I believe, with a lot of persuasion, I would be able to overcome this difficulty. However, I'm very deeply concerned with the attitude of the Muslim authorities in Prijedor, whom I got a chance to talk to at length, and the attitude is until the Serbs of Prijedor come out and tell their story, then they will not encourage or help any witnesses to come to testify. I have even spent a part of an evening having a walk on the main street called Korzo there with the vice-president of the assembly and who has said, "The truth should come out, but perhaps we should wait until other people are either accused or until our pain is relieved, that the guilty are convicted." Your Honour, I have come across four witnesses in Chicago who, having been removed from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vucicevic, couldn't you -- I'm speaking to you in French. I think you can hear me through the interpretation, so let me start again. Couldn't you limit your remarks to the question of the joinder of the case of your client with the other accused, in the case known jointly under the name of Kvocka, without entering into the crux of the subject, because we don't have the time to go into the substance of this matter in five minutes. We are familiar with your arguments. Do you have any other elements to contribute in addition to what you have written regarding the question of joinder, the joinder of this indictment with the affair called Kvocka, that is, the Omarska case? Could you limit your remarks to that? Please be kind enough to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Honourable Judge, in my written submission, that was only a hypothetical possibility that I have given; however, what I am presenting now, that is real. Then by joining Mr. Kolundzija to the others, where the command structure was different, where the witnesses were different, where only a few of the Prosecution witnesses passed from one camp to the other, it will be an extreme prejudice to join this man, who has helped so many and hurt none, to put him in the same lineup where the witnesses who would help you deliver the justice would be taken back by their emotions and not be willing to come forward. That would be an extreme prejudice, not to him but to the justice that this Court could deliver. Because I do know Prijedor. I have cross-examined the whole crisis staff in the previous case. We want -- to deliver the justice, the Court needs counsel who is going to bring as much as possible, and perhaps expediency could take a back seat to justice. I respectfully ask you to do justice in this case and to try my client alone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. This matter now stands adjourned. The next hearing will be announced in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: adjourned at 2.58 p.m. sine die
